passage:
The sociology essay last term was the first one I actually submitted on time. Before that, I'd rewrite introductions until two in the morning and hand things in late with an apology.
This time my lab partner Tanuja watched me start rewriting paragraph one for the third time and said, "Farhan, set a timer. Three hours for the draft, one for fixes. Then it goes."
I hated the idea. But I did it. When the timer rang, the conclusion felt thin, and my hand hovered over the delete key. I submitted anyway, and in a note to myself I wrote: next time, plan the conclusion first, find one more source.
It came back a B-plus with the comment "clear argument". Not perfect. But it was in, I slept, and I knew exactly what to fix next time.

qa.q: How long did Tanuja say Farhan should spend on the draft?
qa.a: Tanuja said three hours for the draft and one for fixes.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when the timer rang and the conclusion felt thin?
qa.a: Farhan felt uneasy and tempted to start over, with a hand hovering over the delete key, because stopping short of perfect felt risky.

qa.q: Which part of Farhan's approach kept the high standard without the stuck feeling?
qa.a: Writing a note on what to improve next time, like planning the conclusion first, kept the standard alive while still letting the essay go in on time.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see the change in Farhan?
qa.a: Tanuja probably feels glad and a little proud, seeing Farhan submit on time and sleep instead of rewriting until two in the morning.

grounding: A student sets a time limit, submits a solid essay and notes what to improve next time, keeping standards without paralysis.

passage:
It was the last week of March, year-end close, and the finance floor ran on chai and tea biscuits. Vidya had finished the vendor report on Monday. By Thursday she was still adjusting column widths and rewording footnotes.
At the review, Mohit presented his version of the cash summary, rough but on time. The director nodded. "Quick work, Mohit. This is what we needed today."
Vidya's report, cleaner and more accurate, arrived that evening. "Thanks," the director wrote. "We'd already decided using Mohit's."
She sat in the empty office after eight. Her sister had messaged twice about dinner; she hadn't answered. She opened the report again and noticed a misaligned decimal on page six. Her jaw tightened. She fixed it, though no one would read that page now.

qa.q: When had Vidya finished the vendor report?
qa.a: Vidya had finished the vendor report on Monday.

qa.q: What does Vidya's tightened jaw suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: She feels frustrated and overlooked, perhaps resentful, because her careful work arrived too late while Mohit's rough version got the praise.

qa.q: What could Vidya try on the next report?
qa.a: She could agree a deadline with herself, send a solid version on time and keep a short list of polish items for later if they matter.

qa.q: How might Vidya's sister be affected by her habit?
qa.a: Her sister gets ignored messages about dinner, so she may feel pushed aside and worried about how much Vidya is working.

grounding: An adult keeps polishing a report past the point needed, loses credit to a faster colleague and sacrifices rest and family time.

passage:
Note left on the flat's kitchen table, Sunday night. Lokesh here.
Shreya, I've watched this for two weeks, so hear me out. You skipped Priti's birthday. You cancelled badminton twice. I've heard you typing at three in the morning. Tonight you told me the design deck "isn't ready" because one icon is two pixels off.
I looked at it while you were in the shower. Sorry. It's good. It's really good.
So here's what I'm doing: tomorrow at eight I'll sit with you for an hour and we'll treat it as a rough-but-fine version, not a final. We mark only the things a client would notice. Then you send it, and we go get dosas.
I'll make the coffee.

qa.q: What did Shreya say was wrong with the design deck?
qa.a: Shreya said one icon is two pixels off.

qa.q: How can you tell Lokesh is worried about Shreya?
qa.a: Lokesh feels concerned enough to track two weeks of missed plans and late-night typing, and even looks at the deck to check how good it is.

qa.q: Why might sitting together for an hour help Shreya?
qa.a: Having company and marking only what a client would notice makes sending an imperfect deck feel survivable instead of frightening for Shreya.

qa.q: What might Shreya feel on reading the note?
qa.a: Shreya might feel embarrassed at being noticed, but also relieved and cared for, since Lokesh thinks the work is good and will sit alongside for an hour.

grounding: A flatmate notices Shreya cancelling plans and losing sleep over tiny flaws and offers to review the work together as a good enough draft.

passage:
The Navratri fair in the village had ended on Saturday, but on Tuesday Aparna was still stuck on it. At the garba circle she had called Damini's new cousin "aunty" by mistake. He was nineteen. Everyone had laughed, and she had laughed too loudly.
Walking to school along the canal, she replayed it. If I had said bhaiya. If I had just stayed quiet. She pictured the cousin telling his friends. She pictured the whole village remembering.
"You're doing it again," Damini said. "Your face is doing the thing."
"Everyone thinks I'm an idiot."
"Honestly, he forgot by the next song. He asked me for your recipe for the chana."
Aparna didn't hear it. She was already back at the garba circle, choosing a different word for the fortieth time, and each time it stung a little more.

qa.q: What did Aparna call Damini's new cousin by mistake?
qa.a: She called him "aunty" by mistake.

qa.q: Why does Aparna keep replaying the moment?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed and anxious, and replaying it feels like fixing it, though each round only makes the sting worse.

qa.q: What could Aparna try when the replay starts?
qa.a: She could notice the loop, remind herself what Damini said about the cousin forgetting, and turn her attention to the walk or a chat with Damini.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Aparna doesn't hear her reassurance?
qa.a: Damini may feel frustrated and a bit helpless, since her good news about the cousin doesn't seem to reach Aparna.

grounding: A teenager replays an awkward remark from a village fair for days, imagining everyone still thinks of it, and the replay deepens the sting.

passage:
14 April, Baisakhi
Everyone at home is at the gurdwara and then the mela. I said I had a headache. I didn't. I just kept looking at the result: FAIL, Organic Chemistry.
Why? Why did I fail when I studied? Was it the second half? Was it me? Maybe I'm just not a science person. Maybe Nitin was right that I only got into this course because of luck. No, he never actually said that. Did he?
Nitin texted: "Jasleen, the resit form closes Friday. Want to fill it together?" I read it three times and then went back to asking why.
It's nine at night now. I have written "why" in this diary eleven times. I have not opened the resit form. I feel worse than this morning.

qa.q: When does the resit form close?
qa.a: The resit form closes Friday.

qa.q: What is Jasleen feeling after a whole day of asking why?
qa.a: Jasleen feels low and stuck, even worse than in the morning, because asking why over and over hasn't led to any plan.

qa.q: What small step could Jasleen take right now?
qa.a: Jasleen could reply to Nitin and fill in the resit form together, then list which topics in the second half need work.

qa.q: What is it like for Nitin when Jasleen doesn't answer?
qa.a: Nitin reached out with a practical offer, so the silence might leave Nitin worried or unsure whether the help was welcome.

grounding: A student who failed a paper keeps asking why and what it means about them, makes no plan, and ends the day feeling lower.

passage:
The rain started just as Sarika reached the café, and then the power went, so the two friends sat by the window with their chai going cold in the grey light.
Salma was on the job rejection again. It had been three weeks. "They said I was the strongest candidate until the last round. So what happened? Was it the salary question? Was it my accent?"
Sarika had heard these exact questions every weekend. She noticed that Salma looked more tired each time, not less. Talking it over wasn't helping; it was just digging.
She waited until Salma paused. "Can I ask something different? What's one small thing that might help this week?"
Salma blinked. The generator kicked in and the fans started again. "I don't know," she said slowly. "Maybe asking them for feedback. I never did."

qa.q: How long ago had Salma's job rejection happened?
qa.a: It had been three weeks.

qa.q: What did Sarika notice that made her change the conversation?
qa.a: Sarika felt concerned, noticing that Salma looked more tired each time, so the talking was giving no relief.

qa.q: Why was Sarika's question a useful step?
qa.a: Asking about one small step for this week moved Salma from repeating why to thinking about an action, like asking for feedback.

qa.q: How might Salma see Sarika's question at first?
qa.a: Salma might be surprised or thrown, since she expected to go over the same questions, but it also seemed to open a new idea.

grounding: A friend notices that rehashing a disappointment brings no relief and gently asks what small step might help now.

passage:
The flour mill in Alka's small town shut at five, and by six the argument with her supervisor was playing in her head for the tenth time. She was sitting on the back step, not shelling the peas she'd bought.
She knew this feeling. She took the notebook from the kitchen shelf and wrote it out: He said I was careless in front of everyone. I think he was unfair. I'll think about it properly tomorrow, 7 pm, fifteen minutes.
Then she closed the book, washed the peas and started the pulao, stirring onions until they turned gold. Her mind went back once; she let it pass and chopped the coriander.
When Nazia came over later, Alka said, "It still bothers me." Nazia nodded. "If it ever starts following you all day, or gets dark, talk to someone trained, okay?" Alka agreed.

qa.q: When did Alka plan to think about the argument properly?
qa.a: She planned to think about it tomorrow, 7 pm, fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling when she sat on the back step?
qa.a: She felt hurt and upset about being called careless in front of everyone, stuck replaying it.

qa.q: Which steps helped Alka break the loop that evening?
qa.a: She wrote the thought down, set a short time for it later, and then did something absorbing by cooking the pulao.

qa.q: How does Nazia see Alka's way of handling it?
qa.a: Nazia seems to support it while caring enough to add that Alka should talk to someone trained if the thoughts start following her all day or get dark.

grounding: An adult notices she is ruminating, writes the thought down, schedules a short time for it and cooks, while a friend mentions professional help if it worsens.

passage:
It was the first snowy night of December in Tallinn, and the Advent candle had been blown out. Jana lay under the blanket, eyes open.
What if I forget my lines at the school concert? What if Mum's bus slides on the ice tomorrow? What if something happens and nobody tells me?
Her stomach went tight. She kicked the blanket off, cross at her own head for not stopping.
The door creaked. Mum, whose name was Esther and who sang in the kitchen, sat on the bed. "Big thoughts?"
Jana nodded and told her. Esther didn't laugh. "My bus has good tyres and a careful driver. And the concert, we'll practise at breakfast." She did their usual thing: three slow breaths, then naming three nice things from the day.
By the third nice thing, Jana's eyes were closing.

qa.q: What did Jana worry might happen to Mum's bus?
qa.a: She worried Mum's bus might slide on the ice tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Jana kick the blanket off?
qa.a: She felt anxious, with a tight stomach, and angry at her own head for not stopping the what-ifs.

qa.q: Which part of Esther's response helped Jana settle?
qa.a: Listening without laughing, giving calm reassurance and doing the usual routine of three breaths and three nice things helped Jana feel calm.

qa.q: What is it like for Esther to find Jana awake?
qa.a: Esther probably feels caring and gentle, taking the worries seriously and wanting to help Jana feel safe enough to sleep.

grounding: A child lies awake with what-ifs about failing and her mother's safety, and a calm routine with reassurance helps.

passage:
Dear Jagdish Veerji,
Mummy says you're coming home for Lohri, so I'm writing before the bonfire and the relatives.
Pre-boards start in three weeks. Every night I sit down with the physics book and my brain starts a list: What if I blank on numericals? What if the paper is from the chapters I skipped? What if I get less than Simar and everyone compares? What if I don't get into any college?
By the time the list ends it's eleven and I've read one page. It feels like worrying is at least doing something. Like if I stop worrying, I've stopped caring.
You went through this. Did you ever feel like this? How did you actually start?
Save me some gajak.
Gurleen

qa.q: When do Gurleen's pre-boards start?
qa.a: Pre-boards start in three weeks.

qa.q: Why does Gurleen keep worrying instead of studying?
qa.a: Gurleen feels anxious and responsible, as if worrying is doing something and stopping would mean not caring, so the list replaces actual study.

qa.q: What would you advise Gurleen for tonight's study time?
qa.a: Gurleen could write the worries down in two minutes, set them aside, and start with one small task such as five physics numericals.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Veerji feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jagdish Veerji may feel protective and understanding, recognising the feeling from past exams and wanting to help Gurleen take the first step.

grounding: A teenager lists every way the exams could go wrong and barely starts studying, because worrying feels like being responsible.

passage:
Durga Puja week, and the girls' hostel was half empty. Manjula, a first-year, had joined the same college as her older sister Disha, and they shared a room this term.
Disha, in final year, checked the door lock three times before bed. She refreshed the placement portal every few minutes. "What if they call and I miss it?" she said, again.
By Thursday, Manjula found herself getting up to check the lock too. She kept her phone face up on the pillow. She had never done that at home. Her chest felt tight for no reason she could name.
On Friday the warden, passing their room, sat down with them. Manjula said it first: "I think I'm catching Didi's worry." Disha went quiet, then laughed shakily. They agreed on a plan: lock checked once, portal at lunch and at six, and phones on the desk at night.

qa.q: How many times did Disha check the door lock before bed?
qa.a: Disha checked the door lock three times before bed.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling by Thursday?
qa.a: Manjula felt tense and uneasy, with a tight chest she couldn't explain, after picking up Disha's worry.

qa.q: What helped the sisters ease the tension?
qa.a: Talking honestly with the warden and agreeing on a clear routine, one lock check, portal twice a day, phones on the desk, lightened it.

qa.q: How might Disha feel when Manjula says she is catching Didi's worry?
qa.a: Disha may feel surprised and a little guilty that her worry was spreading, but also relieved to talk about it openly.

grounding: A younger sister sharing a room picks up her anxious sister's checking habits, and honest talk plus a clear routine lighten it.
